newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Hanson calls for referendum on Australian immigration.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Hanson calls for referendum on Australian immigration.

text.p: Pauline Hanson, the maverick politician who sparked a national debate on immigration, defiantly challenged her parliamentary foes on Thursday to call a referendum on whether Australia should accept more immigrants.

The day after major political parties, hoping to bury a damaging race row, passed a resolution in parliament condemning racism, Queensland MP Hanson said immigration should be immediately halted until unemployment fell to manageable levels.

"There should be a moratorium on all immigration until we clean up our own back yard and get our unemployment down to five percent," Hanson told parliament. Australia's jobless rate is currently running at close to nine percent.
"I am not saying that I want all Asian immigration to cease. There has always been an Asian presence in Australia, always will be. And all I want is the balance restored," Hanson said.

"If the members of this house are so confident that they are echoing the views of mainstream Australia, they should let mainstream Australia have its say. I call on the government to have a referendum on immigration and multiculturalism."

Australia has been embroiled in an emotional national debate on race since Hanson, a fish-and-chip shop owner from northern Australia, made her maiden parliamentary speech seven weeks ago and charged that the country risked being swamped by Asians.
Asians make up less than five percent of Australia's population and account for around a quarter of the 100,000-odd immigrants into Australia every year.

Political and business leaders fear the row has begun to tarnish Australia's image in Asia, where newspapers have criticised Prime Minister John Howard for not openly censuring Hanson for her comments.

On Wednesday, with Hanson conspicuous by her absence, both houses of parliament overwhelmingly passed a resolution confirming Australia's commitment to equal rights and to a non-discriminatory immigration policy.
The established parties hoped the resolution would help calm the race row driven by Hanson, an independent.

Interviewed by Australian television earlier on Thursday, Hanson was scathing about the resolution. "It's directly aimed at me -- and I think they're aiming at the people of Australia as well," she said.
Opinion polls have showed that as many as two-thirds of Australians back Hanson's anti-immigration call, although they do not necessarily share her political beliefs.
